transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I keep getting these thoughts that if I miss even one setting, access rule, or warning sign, somebody could get hurt or lose everything. Part of me knows that sounds irrational, but it feels like it would be my fault, and I can’t just let it go.
When these thoughts come up, do you find yourself repeatedly checking things to make sure nothing was missed?

Yes. I’ll reread deployment plans and audit logs over and over, and check door locks repeatedly. I even go back through old messages. Sometimes I count the steps in my head until it feels safe enough. I’ve stayed at the office for hours after everyone else leaves because if I stop before it feels complete, I panic.
Do these repeated thoughts and checking feel unwanted and intrusive to you?

Yes. I don’t want to be thinking about it all the time. It just comes in—like if I missed one setting or warning sign, someone could be hurt or lose everything, and it would be on me. I know that’s not completely rational, but I can’t seem to move past it.
On a typical day, do these thoughts and checking rituals take more than an hour of your time?

Yes, definitely. It’s gotten bad enough that I missed a major cloud migration deadline because I couldn’t bring myself to finish signing off on the decisions. My team has started working around me instead of relying on me. And I’ve stopped going to basketball and salsa nights, which used to keep me grounded.
Do the checking rituals feel excessive or unreasonable to you?

Yeah, I know it’s excessive. I’ll reread the same plans, logs, even old messages over and over, and check the locks repeatedly. Sometimes I count through the steps in my head until it feels safe. But if I stop before it feels complete, I panic, so I can’t just let it go.
Are you doing these checks mainly to stop something bad from happening?

Yes. I’m trying to make sure nothing gets missed or goes wrong. I reread deployment plans and audit logs, check locks and old messages, sometimes count through the steps in my head until it feels safe. If I stop before it feels complete, I panic. I’ve stayed at the office for hours after everyone else left because I couldn’t make myself stop checking.
Even when you’re not feeling panicked about something bad happening, do you generally see yourself as a very perfectionistic, rigid person who feels things must be done exactly the right way?

I’m not sure. I mean, I do like things done properly, but I don’t know that I’d call myself rigid all the time. It’s more that once I start worrying about something, I can’t feel settled unless I’ve checked it enough.
Do you also find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of other parts of life, even when you’re not caught up in checking?
I’m not really sure. Most of the time it’s not like I’m worried about everything—it tends to latch onto a specific thing, and then I can’t stop checking it.
If you could feel completely certain that no harm would come from it, would you want to stop the checking and counting?

Yes, absolutely. I don’t want to spend hours rereading plans or logs, checking locks, going back through old messages, or counting the steps in my head. I’ve stayed at work long after everyone left because I couldn’t stop. If I could really know nothing bad would happen, I’d stop—I just can’t get that feeling of certainty.
When you’re not in the middle of checking, do you spend a lot of time worrying about many different everyday things?
I don’t think so, not across lots of different things. It usually feels more like one specific concern takes over my attention rather than general everyday worrying.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes recurrent intrusive, unwanted thoughts about causing harm by missing a setting, rule, or warning sign, recognizes these fears as excessive/irrational, and performs repetitive checking and mental counting rituals to reduce anxiety and prevent feared harm. These obsessions and compulsions are time-consuming (more than an hour daily) and cause clear occupational and social impairment. Presentation is more consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder than generalized anxiety disorder or obsessive-compulsive personality disorder because the symptoms are ego-dystonic, focused on specific obsessions, and accompanied by compulsive rituals.
